lesson.title: Diminutives & Augmentatives: -ito, -illo & -ón
lesson.subtitle: From poquito and cafecito (-ito) to word-builders bocadillo ('sandwich' < bocado), pesadilla ('nightmare' < pesado), and limón (< lima)

hook.title: Suffixes That Show Affection — and Invent New Words!
hook.content: As highlighted in *The Thinking Method*, Spanish suffixes like -ito/-ita, -illo/-illa, and -ón/-ona do two remarkable things. First, -ito/-ita adds warmth, affection, or softness to everyday speech: un poco ('a little') becomes un poquito ('just a tiny bit'), un momento becomes un momentito ('just a quick second'), and un café becomes un cafecito! Second, -illo/-illa and -ón actually forged brand-new everyday nouns out of simpler roots!

footnotes.title: Why 'Limón' Has an Augmentative '-ón'
footnotes.content: When citrus fruits arrived in Moorish Spain, the smaller green fruit kept the Arabic name lima ('lime'), and speakers added the 'big' suffix -ón to name the larger yellow citrus: el limón ('the big lime')!

pattern.title: Decoding Bocadillo, Pesadilla, and Limón
pattern.content:
Look at the etymological magic:
• la boca ('mouth') → el bocado ('mouthful / bite') + -illo ('little') = el bocadillo ('little mouthful' → a Spanish baguette sandwich)!
• pesado ('heavy', cousin of peso) + -illa = la pesadilla ('the heavy little thing sitting on your chest in sleep' → a nightmare)!
• la lima ('lime') + augmentative -ón ('big') = el limón ('the big lime' → a lemon)!
pattern.trap_note: Why is poquito spelled with 'qu'? Because in Spanish, 'c' before 'i' would sound like /θ/ or /s/, so c changes to qu to protect the hard /k/ sound of poco!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: un poquito, el bocadillo, la pesadilla, el limón, el queso
exercises.meaning: a tiny bit (poco + -ito), a sandwich ('little mouthful': bocado + -illo), a nightmare ('little heavy thing': pesado + -illa), a lemon ('big lime': lima + -ón), cheese
exercises.explanation: -ito adds warmth; -illo/-illa and -ón created everyday vocabulary.

exercises.prompt: Build the Spanish noun for 'sandwich / snack' from 'bocado' ('mouthful', dropping -o) plus the diminutive suffix:
What literal image hides inside 'la pesadilla' ('the nightmare')?
options: pesado ('heavy') + -illa ('a heavy little weight pressing on the sleeper')
exercises.target_answer: pesado ('heavy') + -illa ('a heavy little weight pressing on the sleeper')
exercises.explanation: Folklore pictured a nightmare as a heavy weight (pesado) sitting on your chest while you sleep!
Quiero un bocadillo de queso — de links the sandwich to its filling.

exercises.idea: ask politely for 'a little bit of water, please' using poquito
exercises.target_answer: Un poquito de agua por favor
exercises.meaning: A little bit of water, please
exercises.explanation: Un poquito de agua, por favor — poquito sounds warm and polite across the whole Spanish-speaking world.

summary.outcome: Use affectionate -ito (poquito) and decode lexicalized -illo/-ón nouns (bocadillo, pesadilla, limón).

use_example.german: Quiero un bocadillo de queso y un poquito de agua con limón.
use_example.english: I want a cheese sandwich and a little bit of water with lemon.

summary.takeaway: Spanish diminutives (-ito, -illo) and augmentatives (-ón) express both social warmth and vivid word creation.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([12] The Near Future: ir a): step into future plans with voy a + infinitive.

poquito.english_meaning: a tiny bit, a little bit
poquito.context_phrase: Un poquito de agua, por favor.
poquito.context_translation: A little bit of water, please.
poquito.etymology_derivation: poco + -ito changes c to qu to keep the /k/ sound: poquito.

pesadilla.etymology_derivation: pesado ('heavy', cousin of peso/pensive) + -illa = 'the heavy little thing on your chest in sleep'!

limón.etymology_derivation: In Spanish, la lima is the smaller green lime, and el limón (-ón augmentative) is the larger yellow lemon!

un_poco.etymology_derivation: Latin paucus ('few, little') gives English 'paucity' and Spanish poco.

agua.shift_rule: Latin aqua (takes el in singular for phonetics)
agua.context_translation: I want a glass of water.
agua.etymology_derivation: Feminine noun (las aguas) that takes el in the singular to prevent a collision with stressed initial /a/.

queso.etymology_derivation: Latin cāseus gave English 'casein' and Spanish queso.

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → Spanish café. An international word shared across Europe.
